messages.subject: Problem with truncated data model
parts:
Hi,

I have some strange problem with truncated data model from user guide.  It is not producing expected estimation of any parameters neither mu nor sigma. My testing procedure is as follows.

1. Prepare random vector of observations from normal random generator with parameters (mean=0, sigma =1).
2. Next truncate data when it is greater than 0.
3. Compile and fit model.
4. Instead of expecting estimations near real values I get mu=-0.8, sigma=0.5.

My code in R is:
library(rstan) 

model_code <- '
data {
int<lower=0> N;
real U;
real<upper=U> y[N];
}
parameters{
real mu;
real<lower=0> sigma;
}
model {
for (n in 1:N)
  y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma) T[,U];
}
'
real_data<- rnorm(200)
truncated_data<-real_data[which(real_data<0)]

data <- list(N = length(truncated_data),U=0, y = truncated_data)

fit <- stan(model_code = model_code, data = data)

print(fit)

Could you suggest what am I doing wrong or how can I achieve better estimations?

regards,
Marek Smigielski

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: Problem with truncated data model [+ log CDF?]
parts:
Good call. Totally my bad. And it affects all of
the truncated distributions, not just the upper-bound
only. None of these will work properly until we release
a patched version of Stan (and RStan), which we will do ASAP.

I just pushed a patch to our code repository that
fixes the issue, which is in stan/gm/generator.hpp,
starting on line 1024 or so.

We should set up a model test as the generator isn't
tested otherwise.

I forgot the negation due to the CDF terms being in
the denominator under a log.

An upper-truncated sampling statement

y ~ foo(...) T[,U];

should translate to the C++:

lp__ += foo_log(y,...);
lp__ -= log(foo_cdf(U,...));

Because I inadvertently made the second line here += instead
of -= in the generator, we'll need to test this
through a model.

The other two cases we have are with just a lower
bound, using log1m(x) == log(1 - x), to set

"" T[L,]
lp__ -= log1m(foo_cdf(L,...));

and with both an upper and lower bound,

"" T[L,U]
lp__ -= log(foo_cdf(U,...) - foo_cdf(L,...));

An earlier thread brings up the issue of whether we
should try to be more careful about underflow of the CDF
to 0 or overflow to 1. We could definitely be much
more careful with the arithmetical precision here.

We could really use three compound log-difference CDF
functions for these three cases.

We could then test if the lower bound was less than
the upper bound, something we're currently not doing.
As is, if they're backwards, you'll try to take the log
of a negative number and get an error that way.

- Bob

W dniu wtorek, 4 września 2012 08:43:30 UTC+2 użytkownik Bob Carpenter napisał:
Good call.  Totally my bad.  And it affects all of
the truncated distributions, not just the upper-bound
only.  None of these will work properly until we release
a patched version of Stan (and RStan), which we will do ASAP.

I just pushed a patch to our code repository that
fixes the issue, which is in stan/gm/generator.hpp,
starting on line 1024 or so.

We should set up a model test as the generator isn't
tested otherwise.

I forgot the negation due to the CDF terms being in
the denominator under a log.

An upper-truncated sampling statement

    y ~ foo(...) T[,U];

should translate to the C++:

    lp__ += foo_log(y,...);
    lp__ -= log(foo_cdf(U,...));

Because I inadvertently made the second line here += instead
of -= in the generator, we'll need to test this
through a model.

The other two cases we have are with just a lower
bound, using log1m(x) == log(1 - x), to set

    "" T[L,]
    lp__ -= log1m(foo_cdf(L,...));

and with both an upper and lower bound,

    "" T[L,U]
    lp__ -= log(foo_cdf(U,...) - foo_cdf(L,...));

An earlier thread brings up the issue of whether we
should try to be more careful about underflow of the CDF
to 0 or overflow to 1.  We could definitely be much
more careful with the arithmetical precision here.

We could really use three compound log-difference CDF
functions for these three cases.

We could then test if the lower bound was less than
the upper bound, something we're currently not doing.
As is, if they're backwards, you'll try to take the log
of a negative number and get an error that way.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Problem with truncated data model [+ log CDF?]
parts:
On 9/4/12 5:47 AM, Marek Smigielski wrote:

> I've just checked source version and still something
> is suspicious in my opinion. Except of strange estimated parameter
> values I get some exceptions.

The strange parameter values, assuming these aren't
what you were expecting, may be due to the model.
Let us fix the underlying distributions first, then we
can circle back and help fix the model if there are
still issues.

We're about to run some tests and release
a revised version of Stan and RStan.

The kinds of errors you're reporting below are
not fatal. They occur when values underflow or
overflow out of range. The sampler treats these
as zero probabilty and goes on its merry way.

If you only see a few, as you did here, it's not
a problem. We're also working on making that
clear by changing "Error" to "Warning" in the report.
(What would be really nice is to link them back to
a line of the Stan source, but that's MUCH trickier
and not on our short-term to-do list.)

In general if you rebuild from source, you need to also
rebuild RStan, because RStan has the Stan code
built into it.

Circling back to your model:

> > data {
> > int<lower=0> N;
> > real U;
> > real<upper=U> y[N];
> > }
> > parameters{
> > real mu;
> > real<lower=0> sigma;
> > }
> > model {
> > for (n in 1:N)
> > y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma) T[,U];
> > }

First, you probably want a proper prior on sigma and on mu.
While Stan doesn't require a proper prior, it does require
a proper posterior.

Because the truncation point is data, it's not
actually doing anything in this model! The data
are all known and constrained to be < U, so
T[,U] terms just add some constants of proportionality.

In order to properly estimate a truncated distribution,
you need to know the number of censored or truncated points.
See Gelman et al.'s Bayesian Data Analysis or Gelman and Hill's
regression book for information on how to code this kind
of thing into a model.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Problem with truncated data model [+ log CDF?]
parts:
I don't think it's a bug --- I just think this
is a very hard model to fit for three reasons:

1. You have improper priors on mu and sigma, which
gives the posterior a lot of latitude in these parameters.

2. Given mu, there's not much constraint on sigma because
of the truncation. As sigma gets larger, the distribution
just gets flatter, but it starts out pretty flat, which
is related to 3.

3. You don't have much data given that you're constraining
centered at +/- 1 sd, which gives you a relatively flat
distribution.

I constrained sigma to the interval (0,10) but left
the improper prior on mu, and it fits fine with 2000
rnorm generations (about 1400 actual data points).

If you only provide 1000 draws from rnorm (700 data points),
the traceplot has a lot of outliers for mu (and hence for sigma, which
follows it). You could potentially run many more iterations,
because the posterior mode looks right in the traceplots.
With 10K iterations/chain, you start to see the right value
for mu, but the posterior's still very broad for sigma.

You can try to control the problem with better priors on
sigma or mu or more data. But otherwise, I think Stan's doing
the right thing.

- Bob

R code
===================================
library('rstan');

set.seed(1234)
mu <- 1;
sigma <- 2;
y <- rnorm(2000, 1, 2);

L <- -1
U <- 3
y <- y[y >= L & y <= U]
N <- length(y)

Il 10/09/2013 21:20, Bob Carpenter ha scritto:
> I don't think it's a bug --- I just think this
> is a very hard model to fit for three reasons:
>
> 1. You have improper priors on mu and sigma, which
> gives the posterior a lot of latitude in these parameters.
>
> 2. Given mu, there's not much constraint on sigma because
> of the truncation. As sigma gets larger, the distribution
> just gets flatter, but it starts out pretty flat, which
> is related to 3.
>
> 3. You don't have much data given that you're constraining
> centered at +/- 1 sd, which gives you a relatively flat
> distribution.
>
> I constrained sigma to the interval (0,10) but left
> the improper prior on mu, and it fits fine with 2000
> rnorm generations (about 1400 actual data points).
>
> If you only provide 1000 draws from rnorm (700 data points),
> the traceplot has a lot of outliers for mu (and hence for sigma, which
> follows it). You could potentially run many more iterations,
> because the posterior mode looks right in the traceplots.
> With 10K iterations/chain, you start to see the right value
> for mu, but the posterior's still very broad for sigma.
>
> You can try to control the problem with better priors on
> sigma or mu or more data. But otherwise, I think Stan's doing
> the right thing.
>
> - Bob

I think it's an interesting case study. We've had
a few instances like this where simulated data didn't
fit well. I meant difficult model in the sense that
you need a lot of data to fit it well with Bayesian
methods --- sometimes point estimates will do the right
thing for these models.

- Bob
